name: Open book
why: Turns the mid back, which stiffens with sitting. A mobile mid back takes strain off both the neck and the lower back.
setup: Lie on your side with hips and knees bent to 90 degrees, arms straight out in front, palms together.
cues: Open your top arm like a book
Follow your hand with your eyes
Keep your knees together
mistakes: Forcing the arm to the floor
feel: A stretch across the chest and a turning movement in the mid back.
stopIf: Pain shoots down an arm or leg.

name: Thread the needle
why: Rotates the mid back from hands and knees and gently stretches the back of the shoulder.
setup: Get on hands and knees, hands under shoulders and knees under hips.
cues: Slide one arm under your body
Let that shoulder and your head lower
Then reach the arm up to the ceiling
feel: A turning movement and stretch in the mid back and the back of the shoulder.
stopIf: Sharp shoulder pain, or pain into the arm.

name: Mid-back extension on a foam roller
why: Arching the mid back over a roller reverses the rounded desk posture and helps the shoulders lift overhead more easily.
setup: Lie on your back with a foam roller across your mid back, just below the shoulder blades, knees bent and feet flat.
Support your head with your hands, elbows pointing forward.
cues: Keep your hips on the floor
Arch gently back over the roller
Try a spot a little higher too
mistakes: Letting the head drop back unsupported
feel: Pressure and a stretch through the mid back.
stopIf: Lower-back pain, or pain spreading around the ribs.

name: Mid-back extension over a chair
why: A desk-friendly way to arch the mid back and undo hours of leaning towards a screen.
setup: Sit on a chair whose backrest reaches about the bottom of your shoulder blades.
Hands behind your head, elbows pointing forward.
cues: Lean back over the top of the chair
Lift your chest towards the ceiling
Keep your hips on the seat
feel: A stretch through the mid back.
stopIf: Lower-back pain or pain into the arms.

name: Y and T raise (lying face down)
why: Strengthens the middle and lower trapezius, the muscles that hold your shoulder blades back and down and support good posture.
setup: Lie face down with a folded towel under your forehead.
Arms overhead in a Y shape, thumbs pointing up. Switch to a T (arms out to the sides) for the second set.
cues: Lift your arms just off the floor
Draw your shoulder blades down
Keep your neck long
feel: Work between and below the shoulder blades.
stopIf: Shoulder pinching or pain into the arm.

name: Wall angel
why: Combines a chest stretch with shoulder-blade control. A good posture reset after long sitting.
setup: Stand with your back against a wall, feet a small step away from it.
Arms in a goalpost shape against the wall.
cues: Slide your arms up the wall
Keep your lower back gently on the wall
Slide down slowly
mistakes: Forcing the arms to touch the wall
feel: A stretch across the chest and work between the shoulder blades.
stopIf: Pain or tingling in the arms.

name: Band pull-apart
why: Strengthens the back of the shoulders and upper back, balancing out all the time spent reaching forward.
setup: Hold a light band in both hands, arms straight in front at shoulder height, hands shoulder-width apart.
cues: Pull the band apart to your chest
Squeeze your shoulder blades
Return slowly
feel: Work at the back of the shoulders and between the shoulder blades.
